options.A: Cut the whole order as The True Diamond -- a symmetric rhombus frame that needs a tail on every kite
options.B: Cut the whole order as The Eddy Flyer -- the historic off-center kite frame that flies tailless

reinforcement_note: The spine has ZERO skills at n==0 (readmodel/standards_spine.json totals.uncovered == 0, reconfirmed at authoring time 2026-09-09 -- no id anywhere in the spine has n==0, and no geometry skill is n==0 either). So this case cannot close a true gap, and claiming geometry-parallelogram, geometry-rhombus, and geometry-kite as new_coverage[] (each already at n=1: parallelogram covered_by 'The Irregular Boundary', rhombus and kite covered_by 'Plaza Pavers') would be padding, not gap-closure -- corrected from an earlier draft that made exactly this claim. Checked the adjacent uncovered geometry skills for anything this case's real deliverables might naturally force instead: there are none -- the entire domain is already at n>=1, so there is no n==0 skill of any kind to route to. This case's real math -- The True Diamond's spine/spreader crossing at the exact midpoint (equal diagonals bisecting each other, the rhombus case) versus The Eddy Flyer's off-center 19%-down crossing (unequal-length diagonal segments, the kite case), both built from the shared parallelogram/quadrilateral diagonal-crossing-and-area relationships in D1-D2 -- is squarely the same geometry the domain already has real coverage for. Publishing as a reinforcement case: de-singletons three fragile n=1 skills to n=2 (parallelogram, rhombus, kite), each exercised by only one other case today, with a genuinely different real-world story (kite manufacturing/material yield) for variety and resilience against any single case being revised or retired later.

deliverables.text: A dimensioned diagram of each frame (spine/spreader as diagonals, crossing point marked); classify Option A as a Rhombus and Option B as a Kite via side-length arithmetic, including which diagonal bisects which.
Sail area of each option via the diagonals formula; state whether the areas are equal or different and why.
Nest two Option A sail panels into a single Parallelogram cutting pattern; verify opposite sides parallel/congruent; confirm its area equals exactly twice one sail's area (zero waste).
Fabric area consumed per kite for each option (sail plus tail where used, per Appendix E's cutting-layout assumption), converted to roll yardage.
Full material cost table per kite and for the 250-kite run (fabric + spar + tail); state which option wins on total material cost and by how much.

balance.argument_a: The True Diamond's rhombus sail is provably the zero-waste cut: two panels nested via 180-degree edge rotation form an exact parallelogram equal to twice the sail's own area (D3), so its fabric use per kite is just the raw 648 sq in sail plus MA1/MA2's tail (576 sq in) = 1,224 sq in, costing $4.505 in fabric. Even needing a tail every real diamond-kite retailer says it needs, its total material cost of $12.005/kite beats Option B by a real (if thin) 2.16%.
balance.argument_b: The Eddy Flyer needs zero tail material at all -- a real, sourced fact about its bowed, off-center-crossing design (S3/S4) -- and its raw sail area is provably identical to Option A's (648 sq in, D2's diagonals-formula result). Its only real cost disadvantage is MA3, a stated (not sourced) assumption that its cutting layout can't achieve the rhombus's zero-waste pairing and must be individually boxed at double the raw sail area. That assumption is soft: the sensitivity model shows Option B would win outright if its real-world cutting waste came in below about 1.89x raw sail area, well within reach of a better cutting layout -- the kind of thing Challenge 1's research could genuinely turn up.
balance.margin_basis: Total material cost per kite (fabric, by cutting-layout efficiency, plus spar plus tail where used) for both options at the 250-kite run size, computed in cases/kite-cut/sensitivity_model.py from Appendix A/B/C/D/E figures.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Tail length for Option A, as a multiple of the kite's own height
modeling_assumptions.basis: Kite-making guidance suggests starting a tail at roughly 3-4x the kite's height and testing from there [S6]; a corroborating hobbyist source says 'several times the height' without an exact number [S7]. No single fixed industry ratio exists.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Scales Option A's tail cost linearly; on its own it does not decide the overall winner (see MA3).

modeling_assumptions.basis: No public standard exists for a giveaway kite's tail width; 4 in is a common, easy-to-cut craft strip width cut from the same fabric roll as the sail.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Scales Option A's tail cost linearly, same as MA1.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Cutting-layout efficiency for Option B's sail panels
modeling_assumptions.value_used: Individually boxed inside a 36 in x 36 in bounding square -- no pairing efficiency (2x the raw sail area)
modeling_assumptions.basis: The zero-waste parallelogram pairing proven for Option A (D3) relies on the rhombus's point symmetry. The Eddy sail's off-center crossing point breaks that symmetry, so the same simple two-panel pairing does not close into a clean shape; this case assumes the simpler individually-boxed layout rather than a researched interlocking cut.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The case's most sensitive assumption -- the sensitivity model shows Option B would overtake Option A on total material cost if its real cutting-layout waste multiplier fell below about 1.89x raw sail area (stated value is 2.0x). Every quadrilateral can, in principle, tile a plane with zero gaps, so a better real cutting layout for the kite shape is a live possibility, not a closed question.

sensitivity_note: MA3 is genuinely close to flipping the case: at the stated 2.0x waste multiplier Option A wins by 2.16%, but the sensitivity model's own flip-point search shows Option B would win outright below about a 1.89x multiplier -- a gap of roughly 6%. MA1/MA2 (tail length and width) only scale Option A's tail cost and are not independently load-bearing at the stated values -- but a Tier-2 P5 assumption-flex sweep (+/-50% on all three dials) shows all three CAN flip the verdict at the extremes: tail_len_mult and tail_width_in flip at +50% (6x height / 6in width), and b_layout_waste_mult flips at -50% (1.0x). See sensitivity_disclosure[] for the per-param disclosure this triggers.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: MA1's own basis states no single fixed industry ratio exists for kite-tail length -- sources [S6][S7] give a 3-4x-height starting range and 'test from there,' not a discoverable true value. A +50% flex to 6x height sits outside any cited guidance and flips the verdict to B, but no amount of research recovers a single correct ratio to cite instead; this is a design choice, not an unresearched fact.

MA2's basis states no public standard exists for a giveaway kite's tail-strip width; 4in was chosen as a common craft-strip width. A +50% flex to 6in flips the verdict to B, but like MA1 there is no single true width to discover through more research -- it is a maker's design choice within a wide workable range.

The true achievable cutting-layout efficiency for the Eddy sail's kite-shaped panels is knowable in principle (a real cutting-floor test or an interlocking-tessellation study could establish it) but not publicly documented for this specific shape, so MA3 uses a documented, conservative good-faith estimate (individually-boxed, no pairing) rather than an unresearched guess. A -50% flex to 1.0x flips the verdict to B and is exactly the live possibility MA3's own sensitivity note and Appendix H's research questions already point Heroes toward -- this is the case's central, disclosed fragility, not a hidden one.
